nodes.name: Willow
nodes.desc: Shrubby willows grow in thickets on river bars and in alpine heath. Moose browse the fresh shoots, and Wikipedia says the park's moose are often seen in dense willow.

nodes.name: Cowberry
nodes.desc: A low evergreen berry shrub of spruce forest and tundra. Ravens and common redpolls are recorded eating its berries, and bears eat berries in general.

nodes.name: Grasses and sedges
nodes.desc: Grasses and sedges grow in alpine meadows, subalpine slopes and wet muskeg. Dall sheep graze them in summer and dig out frozen stems in winter.

nodes.name: Fireweed
nodes.desc: A tall wildflower that moves into burned or bare ground. Bumble bees are recorded visiting its flowers in the park area.

nodes.name: Lichens
nodes.desc: Slow-growing ground lichens, including reindeer lichen, are a staple winter food for caribou, which dig down through snow to reach them.

nodes.name: Ocean plankton
nodes.desc: Drifting plants and animals in the Gulf of Alaska. Sockeye feed mainly on zooplankton at sea and build up the energy stores they carry upstream.

nodes.name: Dall sheep
nodes.desc: Graze grasses, sedges and willow on steep alpine ground. Wikipedia lists wolves, coyotes and bears as main predators and golden eagles as predators of young. The park holds one of the densest populations on the continent.

nodes.name: Caribou
nodes.desc: Winter feeding leans on lichens that they reach by digging through snow. The park is home to the Mentasta and Chisana herds.

nodes.name: Moose
nodes.desc: Browse willow, birch and forbs, and aquatic plants in summer. Wolves are the main predator, brown bears take mostly calves, and fire-disturbed forest grows good moose fodder.

nodes.name: Snowshoe hare
nodes.desc: Eats grasses and herbs in summer and woody twigs and buds, including willow, in winter. Lynx are its most important predator and the two rise and fall together.

nodes.name: Sockeye salmon
nodes.desc: Feeds mostly on zooplankton at sea, then stops eating when it returns to fresh water to spawn. Its carcasses carry ocean nutrients inland.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: An opportunistic bird that eats berries, small birds and carrion, and is among the commonly recorded birds of the park.

nodes.name: Bald eagle
nodes.desc: The best-recorded bird of prey in the area. Takes fish such as spawning salmon, and GloBI also records it eating ravens and other birds.

nodes.name: Golden eagle
nodes.desc: A powerful hunter of open mountain country. Preys on young Dall sheep and on hares, and GloBI records it eating ravens.

nodes.name: Canada lynx
nodes.desc: A boreal cat that depends on snowshoe hares, its most important prey, and rises and falls with their roughly ten-year cycle.

nodes.name: Wolverine
nodes.desc: A solitary mountain scavenger that eats a lot of carrion, including the remains of moose and caribou killed by other predators.

nodes.name: Gray wolf
nodes.desc: Packs hunt moose, caribou and, in the mountains, Dall sheep, and smaller animals add to the diet. Their kills feed ravens, wolverines and bears.

nodes.name: Grizzly bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats mostly plants and berries, fishes for salmon and takes moose and caribou, mainly calves and weak animals. Bears carry salmon inland and spread ocean nitrogen to the forest.

nodes.name: Short summer sun
nodes.desc: Summers are brief but long-lit, and growth is packed into about two months.

nodes.name: Wildfire
nodes.desc: Fire shapes which trees dominate. Aspen and birch return first after a burn, which creates fresh browse for moose.

nodes.name: Glacial rivers
nodes.desc: Glaciers cover a large part of the park and feed the silty rivers that salmon run up from the coast.

nodes.name: Cold soils and nutrients
nodes.desc: Permafrost and cold slow decay, so nutrients recycle slowly. Salmon carcasses add marine nitrogen along streams.

nodes.name: Fungi and soil microbes
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, carcasses and spawned-out salmon and return nutrients to the soil.
